# Results (generated by `pipeline/05_summary.py` - do not edit by hand)

Objective, all stages: k=20 seeds, IC p=0.12, 80 sims per evaluation; winners re-evaluated with 400 fresh sims. Graph: Higgs retweet WCC, 223,833 nodes / 308,596 edges, edges oriented retweeted -> retweeter.

Shared baselines: top-degree **8012.5** (4000 sims; 30x150-sim reps: 8013.2 ± 18.7); random seeds 31.5 ± 31.6.

## Stage-specific controls

- **Heuristics (stage 1):** Top-degree 8012.5, Top-PageRank 6162.1, Top-k-core 2517.2, Random seeds 31.5.
- **CELF (stage 2):** lazy greedy on 200 fixed live-edge snapshots over the top-3000 out-degree pool; snapshot estimate 8028.2, fresh 400-sim 8003.5 (-0.11% vs top-degree; set-level t=-1.21, p=0.23); shares 20/20 seeds with top-degree.
- **Decoder-only (stage 4):** z=0 (no BO bias), diversity weight swept on an 11-point grid; best fresh 8028.4 (+0.20% vs top-degree; set-level p=0.61). BO runs above decoder-only: 0/5.
- **Stage 3 pool:** 593 embedded nodes; 19/20 top-degree seeds are inside it.

## How to read the p-values

The set-level Welch test compares Monte Carlo estimates of two *fixed* seed sets. It supports "this particular seed set spreads more/less than top-degree", not "BO beats top-degree". Method-level evidence is the run-level columns: mean ± sd across independent BO runs and how many runs beat top-degree.
